title: A Wife Remembers Or On the Kind of Husband Who Won't Be Forgot
author: Michael Foster
summary: Foster resurrects Lucy Hutchinson's seventeenth-century memoir of her husband, Colonel John Hutchinson, using modernized language to showcase her reverent appreciation of a man who was simultaneously strong and tender. The portrait shows Hutchinson as physically graceful, intellectually cultured, morally steadfast (resistant to religious persecution), and devoted to his wife in a way that deepened as she aged—a model Foster holds up as countercultural to contemporary marriage. The piece argues for revival of such deliberate, unapologetic honor between spouses, suggesting that a woman's fierce commitment to esteeming her husband serves not only him but their children and the broader culture of what husbands can actually be.
points: A man can be both strong and tender, combining martial skill and discipline with aesthetic appreciation, gentleness, and deep affection—a combination modern culture falsely treats as incompatible.
Marital reverence—a wife's deliberate choice to honor and esteem her husband—is not submissiveness but a powerful cultural statement about what a man can become and what he owes his family.
Real love deepens with time rather than diminishing: Lucy Hutchinson notes her husband's affection intensified as she aged, contradicting the notion that marriage is sustained by youth or novelty.
A man's character is measured not by external status but by how he treats the vulnerable—Hutchinson's courtesy to the poorest soldiers and common laborers marks his true nobility.

Mothers shape what men their sons become by modeling either reverence or contempt for their father—Lucy's insistence that children grow up honoring their father shapes an entire generation's understanding of manhood.
quotes: In the late 1600s, Lucy Hutchinson wrote Memoirs of the Life of Colonel Hutchinson, recounting the life of her late husband, Colonel John Hutchinson of Owthorpe, who had served under Cromwell. It is a reminder that a man can be both tough and tender, and that such a man is worthy of the reverence of a good woman.

As for his love for his wife, anyone who wished to draw up a rule of honor, kindness, and religion needed only to copy his example. No man ever had greater passion for a woman, nor more honorable esteem for a wife. He governed by persuasion, which he used only for what was honorable and good for her.
So steady was his love that when she ceased to be young and lovely, he began to show her the greatest affection.
He showed a sweet and loving courtesy even to the poorest, and often spent many spare hours among common soldiers and poor laborers.

Mrs. Hutchinson's words sometimes edge into hagiography. What stands out is her fierce desire to honor the man she loved and to see her children grow up with the same reverence. The world would be better with more of that.” Archived from We Made People (Foster Substack) on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
